misconceptions.statement: Mangalyaan was launched using a GSLV Mk III rocket.
misconceptions.why: Students link big Indian missions with the biggest rocket.
misconceptions.fix: Mangalyaan was launched by the smaller PSLV-C25 rocket, which put it into an Earth orbit first.

probe.question: Which ISRO rocket launched Mangalyaan?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger mission needs bigger vehicle

misconceptions.statement: Mangalyaan was India's first mission to the Moon.
misconceptions.why: Chandrayaan is more widely remembered and the two missions are mixed up.
misconceptions.fix: Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission) went to Mars, launched in 2013; Chandrayaan-1 (2008) went to the Moon.

probe.question: Which body did Mangalyaan go to?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar names mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Mangalyaan landed on the surface of Mars.
misconceptions.why: Students think reaching a planet means landing on it.
misconceptions.fix: Mangalyaan only orbited Mars; it never landed. It entered orbit on 24 September 2014.

probe.question: Where did Mangalyaan stay after reaching Mars?

misconceptions.root_belief: reaching a place means touching it

misconceptions.statement: Mangalyaan carried a rover to explore Mars.
misconceptions.why: Media pictures of Mars rovers like Curiosity are common.
misconceptions.fix: Mangalyaan was an orbiter with five instruments, including a methane sensor and a camera; it had no rover.

probe.question: What instruments did Mangalyaan use to study Mars?
probe.wrong_answer: A rover that drove on Mars

misconceptions.root_belief: all missions to a planet look the same

misconceptions.statement: Mangalyaan's only purpose was to prove India's technology, not to do science.
misconceptions.why: It is often called a technology demonstrator, so students ignore the science.
misconceptions.fix: Mangalyaan was a technology demonstrator and also carried five science instruments studying Mars' atmosphere and surface.

probe.question: Did Mangalyaan do any scientific study of Mars?

misconceptions.root_belief: a label gives the only purpose

misconceptions.statement: Mangalyaan cost thousands of crores, similar to other planetary missions.
misconceptions.why: Space missions are assumed to be always very expensive.
misconceptions.fix: Mangalyaan cost about ₹450 crore, less than many other Mars missions and less than the budget of some films.

probe.question: About how much did Mangalyaan cost?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger goals always mean bigger numbers

misconceptions.statement: Mangalyaan was cheap because ISRO used poor-quality parts and took risks with safety.
misconceptions.why: Students equate low cost with low quality.
misconceptions.fix: The low cost came from a simple design, reusing existing technology, a small team and using the smaller PSLV with Earth-bound orbit raising.

probe.question: Why was Mangalyaan low cost?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it used cheap, low-quality parts

misconceptions.root_belief: cheaper means worse quality

misconceptions.statement: A spacecraft to Mars is aimed straight at Mars and fired directly there.
misconceptions.why: Students imagine space travel as a straight line like an arrow.
misconceptions.fix: Mangalyaan first orbited Earth, was raised in several steps, then given a push (trans-Mars injection) to follow a curved path to Mars.

probe.question: How did Mangalyaan reach Mars after launch?
probe.wrong_answer: It flew straight to Mars in a straight line

misconceptions.root_belief: moving things travel in straight lines to target
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas about orbits and trajectories in astronomy education

misconceptions.statement: Mangalyaan reached Mars by just continuing its speed and Mars pulled it in on its own.
misconceptions.why: Students think gravity alone always brings a spacecraft into a stable orbit.
misconceptions.fix: The spacecraft had to fire its engine to slow down at the right moment; otherwise it would fly past Mars.

probe.question: Why did Mangalyaan fire its engine near Mars?
probe.wrong_answer: To speed up and crash-land on Mars

misconceptions.root_belief: one force alone explains the whole motion

misconceptions.statement: Slowing a spacecraft near Mars means firing its engine toward the direction of travel is wrong; engines only speed things up.
misconceptions.why: Engines are linked with speeding up.
misconceptions.fix: To slow down, the engine is fired in the direction the craft is moving, so the push acts backward.

probe.question: To slow down, in which direction should a spacecraft fire its thrusters?

misconceptions.root_belief: engine always means going faster

misconceptions.statement: Signals from Mangalyaan reached Earth instantly.
misconceptions.why: Students think radio waves have no travel time.
misconceptions.fix: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, so Mars signals took several minutes to reach Earth.

probe.question: How long did a signal from Mars take to reach Earth?

misconceptions.root_belief: fast means instant
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about the speed of light

misconceptions.statement: There is no gravity near Mars or in space, so the spacecraft just floats.
misconceptions.why: Astronauts and spacecraft seem weightless in videos.
misconceptions.fix: Gravity acts in space; Mars' gravity captures the spacecraft and keeps it in orbit.

probe.question: What holds Mangalyaan in orbit around Mars?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing; there is no gravity in space

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot feel is absent
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about gravity in space (Driver, Nussbaum)

misconceptions.statement: Satellites stay up because they are beyond Earth's gravity.
misconceptions.why: Weightless-looking astronauts suggest gravity is absent.
misconceptions.fix: Satellites feel almost full gravity; they stay up because they move sideways fast enough to keep falling around Earth.

probe.question: Why does a satellite not fall to Earth?
probe.wrong_answer: Gravity does not reach that high

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot feel is absent
misconceptions.source_hint: concept inventories on gravity and orbital motion (misconceptions about weightlessness)

misconceptions.statement: Aditya-L1 is a mission to study the Moon and Earth's weather.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse Aditya-L1 with other ISRO missions.
misconceptions.fix: Aditya-L1 is India's first mission to study the Sun, including its outer layers and solar wind.

probe.question: What does Aditya-L1 study?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar names mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: The Sun is a solid ball with a hard surface that Aditya-L1 observes.
misconceptions.why: Pictures show the Sun as a sharp-edged disc.
misconceptions.fix: The Sun is a giant ball of hot gas (plasma) with no solid surface; the visible photosphere is its glowing layer.

probe.question: Is the Sun solid, liquid or gas?

misconceptions.root_belief: what looks sharp is solid
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas about the Sun and stars

misconceptions.statement: Aditya-L1 has only one instrument, a camera taking pictures.
misconceptions.why: Students imagine a satellite as a single camera.
misconceptions.fix: Aditya-L1 carries seven payloads, including the VELC coronagraph, particle detectors and a magnetometer.

probe.question: How many payloads does Aditya-L1 carry?

misconceptions.root_belief: a satellite is just a camera

misconceptions.statement: L1 is a point very close to the Sun, where Aditya-L1 sits near its surface.
misconceptions.why: Students think a Sun mission must be near the Sun.
misconceptions.fix: L1 is about 1.5 million km from Earth toward the Sun, only about 1% of the Earth-Sun distance.

probe.question: About how far is L1 from Earth?
probe.wrong_answer: Close to the Sun, about 150 million km

misconceptions.root_belief: studying something means being next to it

misconceptions.statement: Aditya-L1 will land on the Sun or fall into it.
misconceptions.why: Students think going toward the Sun means entering it.
misconceptions.fix: Aditya-L1 stays in a halo orbit around L1 and never goes near the Sun; the Sun would destroy any craft.

probe.question: Will Aditya-L1 land on the Sun?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will land on the Sun

misconceptions.root_belief: reaching a place means touching it

misconceptions.statement: At L1 there is no gravity at all because Sun and Earth cancel exactly.
misconceptions.why: Students hear 'balance' and think forces vanish.
misconceptions.fix: Both pulls still act; at L1 their combined pull equals what is needed to keep the craft orbiting along with Earth around the Sun.

probe.question: What is the gravity at L1?

misconceptions.root_belief: balanced forces mean no forces
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student reasoning about balanced and net forces

misconceptions.statement: Aditya-L1 observes the Sun only during the day, like a telescope on Earth.
misconceptions.why: On Earth the Sun is visible only in daytime.
misconceptions.fix: From L1 the Sun is always in view, day and night, with no eclipses blocking it.

probe.question: Can Aditya-L1 watch the Sun at all times?

misconceptions.root_belief: my local view applies everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Aditya-L1 reached L1 in a few days after launch.
misconceptions.why: Students think space travel is fast like on screen.
misconceptions.fix: Aditya-L1 launched on 2 September 2023 and reached L1 on 6 January 2024, about four months later.

probe.question: How long did Aditya-L1 take to reach L1?

misconceptions.root_belief: fast means instant

misconceptions.statement: Sun's UV and X-rays can be studied well from Earth's surface because the Sun is so bright.
misconceptions.why: Students think bright light means all light reaches the ground.
misconceptions.fix: The atmosphere absorbs most UV and X-rays, so they must be observed from space.

probe.question: Why is Aditya-L1 put in space to study the Sun?
probe.wrong_answer: No need; all sunlight reaches the ground

misconceptions.root_belief: what we see is all that exists

misconceptions.statement: The Sun is too hot for Aditya-L1, so it is the heat that makes the mission distance large.
misconceptions.why: Students think heat travels unchanged through space.
misconceptions.fix: Distance matters because L1 gives a stable, uninterrupted view; at 1.5 million km the craft is also far from the Sun's heat, but the main reason for L1 is its stable position.

probe.question: Why is Aditya-L1 placed at L1?
probe.wrong_answer: Only to avoid the Sun's heat

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
